“GET, POST, PUT. It all sounds simple, so why do so many API bugs start right here?”

idea idea Analogy · 8.3s–14.1s

Headline: Ask, then get a number

“Your app sends a verb, what to do, and a path, which thing. The server replies with a number.”

breakdown get Sequence · 14.1s–21.8s

Headline: Just looking

“A GET just reads. Ask for your cart, and the server answers two hundred: all good.”

breakdown post Sequence · 21.8s–27.5s

No headline

“A POST creates something. Place an order, and you get back a two oh one: created.”

breakdown putdelete Sequence · 27.5s–32.9s

Headline: Replace or remove

“A PUT replaces your whole address. A DELETE removes it, and it's gone.”

breakdown twice Split · 32.9s–40.1s

Headline: The double-tap test

“Now send it twice. A PUT twice leaves the same address, but a POST twice makes two orders.”

breakdown retry Decision · 40.1s–51.0s

Headline: Try again?

“That's idempotency. If a request times out, retry freely for GET, PUT and DELETE. For POST, use an idempotency key.”

breakdown codes Tiers · 51.0s–61.9s

No headline

“Codes come in four families. Two hundreds mean it worked, three hundreds look elsewhere, four hundreds are your mistake, and five hundreds are ours.”

breakdown bug Split · 61.9s–69.8s

Headline: The lying 200

“Here's the classic bug. Some APIs answer two hundred even when the work failed, so always read the body, not just the code.”

breakdown cache FlowDiagram · 69.8s–76.2s

Headline: Cache the reads

“Caching? A GET only reads, so a cache can answer. A POST changes things, so it goes to the server.”

gist gist GistCard · 76.2s–81.7s

No headline

“That's the gist: pick the right verb, and answer with the right code. Follow for more.”
